Approximate an arbitrary $v\in H^1_\#(Y)$ in $H^1$ by smooth periodic functions using [F1]; convergence of the derivatives in $L^2(Y)$ implies convergence of their integrals by [F3] and $|Y|=1$. Thus every component of $\int_Y\nabla v$ is zero.

For smooth periodic $v$, write $m=\int_Yv(y)\,dy$. For $x,y\in Y$, telescope from $y$ to $x$ one coordinate at a time. The $i$th difference is the integral of $\partial_i v$ along a segment of length at most one, with the earlier coordinates fixed at $x$ and later coordinates fixed at $y$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F3] bounds its square by the integral of $|\partial_i v|^2$ along the full unit coordinate interval. The inequality $|\sum_{i=1}^d b_i|^2\le d\sum_i|b_i|^2$ and Tonelli [F4], integrating in $x$ and $y$, then give $\int_Y\int_Y|v(x)-v(y)|^2\,dy\,dx\le d\sum_{i=1}^d\|\partial_i v\|_2^2.$ For each $x$, Jensen's inequality gives $|v(x)-m|^2=|\int_Y(v(x)-v(y))dy|^2\le\int_Y|v(x)-v(y)|^2dy$. Integrating in $x$ proves the stated inequality for smooth periodic mean-zero $v$.

Approximate any $v\in V_\#$ in $H^1$ by smooth periodic $v_n$ using Countable Choice [F5]. Their means converge to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, so $v_n-\int_Yv_n$ are smooth periodic mean-zero functions converging to $v$ in $H^1$. Passing to the limit in step 1.2 proves the inequality on $V_\#$. On each such cell choose its lower corner $x_k=\epsilon k$. The mean-value bound gives $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(x_k)|\le\sqrt d\epsilon\|\nabla\varphi\|_\infty$. By change of variables, $\int_{C_k^\epsilon}|g(x/\epsilon)|dx=\epsilon^d\|g\|_{L^1(Y)}$.
